claim_checks.section: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
claim_checks.claim: - Every registered claim is optional in RFC 7519 itself ✅[^1]
claim_checks.page_says: None of the claims defined below are intended to be mandatory to use or implement in all cases
claim_checks.note: RFC 7519 section 4.1; each registered claim's text also ends 'Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.'

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
claim_checks.claim: The lab reproduces it: a token copied before logout was still accepted 60 seconds after the logout, and rejected only after its `exp` ✅[^24]
claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^24] is a local lab file (experiments/jwt-revocation-lab.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.page_says: it makes sense to configure the lifetime of the cookie-based session managed by the BFF to be equal to the maximum lifetime of the refresh token.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 section 6.1.2.2 also says it makes sense to invalidate the session when the BFF learns the refresh token is no longer valid; the row's lower-case 'should' matches this advisory wording.

claim_checks.page_says: When the DPoP proof is used in conjunction with the presentation of an access token in protected resource access (see Section 7), the DPoP proof MUST also contain
claim_checks.note: RFC 9449 section 4.2 requires ath only when the proof accompanies an access token at a protected resource; a proof sent to the AS token endpoint carries no ath. The row (receiver 'AS or RS') lists ath unconditionally while marking only the nonce optional: a dropped condition. Per-request proofs, htm, htu, iat and the short acceptance window (section 11.1) are supported.

claim_checks.claim: optional in RFC 7519 ✅[^1]
claim_checks.page_says: Its value MUST be a number containing a NumericDate value.  Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7519 section 4.1.4 (exp). The claim is the evidence cell 'optional in RFC 7519'.

claim_checks.claim: used by back-channel logout ✅[^9]
claim_checks.page_says: If a sid Claim is not present, the intent is that all sessions at the RP for the End-User identified by the iss and sub Claims be logged out.
claim_checks.note: Back-Channel Logout defines sid as the identifier of one User Agent or device session at the RP, matching the row's 'if absent' cell.

claim_checks.page_says: status_list: REQUIRED when the status mechanism defined in this specification is used.
claim_checks.note: Draft 21 section 6.2: status_list must contain idx (non-negative integer) and uri; the row's structure matches.

claim_checks.page_says: Some browsers use Lax as the default value if SameSite is not specified
claim_checks.note: MDN also gives Strict = same-site only, Lax = also cross-site top-level navigations with a safe method, None = cross-site and same-site with Secure required.

claim_checks.page_says: Cookies with names starting with __Host- must be set with the Secure attribute by a secure page (HTTPS). In addition, they must not have a Domain attribute specified
claim_checks.note: MDN continues: the Path attribute must be set to /. The rules hold in supporting user agents; the doc states that limit in the sentence right after the table.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Threat model: what injected JavaScript can do
claim_checks.claim: The central consequence: the attacker's code is indistinguishable from the app's code, so it can always ask for fresh tokens the way the app does; storage choices only decide whether it can take tokens that already exist ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: the attacker will always be able to request tokens from the provider in exactly the same way as the legitimate application code.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 section 8 continues that storage properties only affect the attacker's ability to obtain existing tokens from storage.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Where the browser can keep a token
claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^25] is a local lab file (experiments/cookie-visibility.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: The claim text '; lab' cites only the local cookie lab. Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Where the browser can keep a token
claim_checks.page_says: localStorage persists between page reloads and is shared across all tabs. This storage is accessible to the entire origin and persists longer term.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 section 8.5: malicious JavaScript can read localStorage and none of the persistent options can fully mitigate exfiltration; OWASP [^13]: a single XSS can steal all data in these objects. The 'sent automatically: No' cell follows from section 8.1, which names cookies as the store that is also a transport mechanism.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Where the browser can keep a token
claim_checks.page_says: Consequently, whenever the application wants to perform an operation with a token, it has to ask the Service Worker to perform this operation and return the result.
claim_checks.note: Sections 8.2 and 8.3: the Service Worker MUST NOT store tokens in persistent storage shared with the main window; a worker does not stop the attacker obtaining new tokens; Web Workers are ephemeral, Service Workers persistent.

claim_checks.claim: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF), where another site makes the browser send a request that carries the cookie, needs a defence ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: Similar to other cookie-based interactions, the BFF is required to account for Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks.
claim_checks.note: The bullets that follow (SameSite=Strict limits with same-site subdomains, custom-header CORS defence with a MUST check on every request, double-submit cookies) match section 6.1.3.3.

claim_checks.claim: What the BFF does and does not stop ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: are effectively mitigated by the BFF application architecture ... nothing will be able to prevent such attacks apart from stopping the execution of malicious code
claim_checks.note: Sections 6.1.4.1 and 6.1.4.2: 5.1.1 to 5.1.3 are mitigated (no tokens in the browser; a confidential client's codes cannot be redeemed without its credentials); proxying (5.1.4) is not.

claim_checks.claim: Storage follows section 4; no option prevents exfiltration once a script runs on the page ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: The attacker is not only able to hijack the client but is also able to extract a full-featured set of tokens from the browser-based application.
claim_checks.note: Section 6.3.4.3 (browser-only client); section 6.3.4.2.1 adds that even storage that completely isolates tokens does not stop a new flow obtaining fresh tokens.

claim_checks.claim: RFC 10017 §7.1 covers the same case, a frontend and backend on one domain with no need for OAuth, and points to a cookie-based session with the cookie rules of §6.1.3.2 ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: Instead of using access tokens, the application can rely on server-side cookie-based session state to keep track of the user's authentication status.
claim_checks.note: Section 7.1 (single-domain apps not using OAuth) then points to the cookie guidelines of section 6.1.3.2.

claim_checks.claim: mitigated ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: The third scenario, where the attacker obtains a fresh access token (and optionally refresh token) by running a silent flow, is mitigated by making the BFF a confidential client.
claim_checks.note: Section 6.1.4.2.

claim_checks.claim: exposed ✅[^25]
claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^25] is a local lab file (experiments/cookie-visibility.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.page_says: the RP locates the session(s) identified by the iss and sub Claims and/or the sid Claim. The RP then clears any state associated with the identified session(s).
claim_checks.note: The pages support ending one login session by sid or by deleting a BFF session, but give no worst-case delay ('same as 6.2': store replication plus local cache time), no per-request cost ('one lookup') and no failure mode ('a session store under another name'). [^2] mentions session replication only as a scalability cost of server-side sessions. Searched both for 'delay', 'replication', 'cache', 'lookup'.

claim_checks.page_says: The issuance of new short-lived session cookies is contingent upon Chrome proving possession of the corresponding private key to the server.
claim_checks.note: The page also says exfiltrated cookies quickly expire and that sites add registration and refresh endpoints. In scope of [^19]'s Rank 1 scope (Chrome DBSC).

claim_checks.claim: Short access tokens limit how long a revoked grant can still be used ✅[^6]
claim_checks.page_says: This allows the authorization server to impose a limit on the time revoked when access tokens are in use.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7009 section 3, about short-lived access tokens refreshed with refresh tokens.

claim_checks.claim: ; an `EXPIREAT` time already in the past deletes the key at once ✅[^16]
claim_checks.page_says: EXPIREAT/PEXPIREAT with a time in the past will result in the key being deleted rather than expired
claim_checks.note: Grounding passes. The clause after the mark ('so revoking an already-expired token stores nothing') applies EXPIREAT behaviour to the doc's SET ... EXAT command; neither Redis page says SET with a past EXAT deletes the key. That clause is not part of the marked claim.

claim_checks.claim: - `EXAT` sets an absolute Unix expiry in seconds ✅[^17]
claim_checks.page_says: Set the specified Unix time at which the key will expire, in seconds (a positive integer).
claim_checks.note: Redis SET, EXAT option.

claim_checks.claim: - **ECDSA signatures.** If (r, s) is a valid ECDSA signature, so is (r, n − s), where n is the curve order; no private key is needed; EdDSA (the Edwards-curve signature family) is not affected ✅[^5]
claim_checks.page_says: n is the order of the subgroup we are working on (aka the order of the generator G) i.e. the number of elements of the subgroup.
claim_checks.note: The page defines n as the order of the subgroup generated by G, not the curve order; the two coincide only for cofactor-1 curves such as P-256, which the page does not state. The (r, n - s) twin, no private key needed and EdDSA not affected are supported. Separately, [^5] is Rank 6 cited in a role 3 section (KB-15 violation).

claim_checks.claim: The author of the malleability write-up reports, among others, that PyJWT 2.13.0 accepted all three non-canonical forms and java-jwt 4.5.2 accepted padding and trailing bits; those library results were not re-tested here ✅[^5]
claim_checks.page_says: | Python | pyjwt | A | A | A | Tested on 2.13.0. ... | Java | java-jwt-4.5.2 | A | R | A | Tested on 4.5.2.
claim_checks.note: Table of parser leniency (columns Padding, Plain Base64, Fill with 1): pyjwt accepts all three; java-jwt accepts padding and trailing bits. Grounding passes; the citation is Rank 6 in a role 3 section (KB-15 violation).

claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^24] is a local lab file (experiments/jwt-revocation-lab.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.claim: Many tokens share one list ("herd privacy"), so the issuer cannot tell which token is being checked; per-token lists would defeat that ✅[^8]
claim_checks.page_says: Therefore, the Issuer does not learn for which Referenced Token the Relying Party is requesting the Status List.
claim_checks.note: Draft 21 section 12.2 adds that generating a unique Status List for every Referenced Token bypasses herd privacy.

claim_checks.claim: The OWASP cheat sheet recommends it for issuer-side revocation ✅[^4]
claim_checks.page_says: you should consider whether there is a better solution for your problem: ... Token Status List is a scalable solution for revocation of the JWT by the issuer.
claim_checks.note: The sheet also opens its 'JWT revocation' section with: if revocation by the issuer is needed, Token Status Lists can be used.

claim_checks.claim: The lab ran five cases ✅[^24]
claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^24] is a local lab file (experiments/jwt-revocation-lab.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.claim: Limits ✅[^11]
claim_checks.page_says: the adversary cannot exfiltrate the key and use it to create arbitrary DPoP proofs. The adversary can, however, create new DPoP proofs as long as the client is online
claim_checks.note: Section 11.4; section 11.2 covers pre-generated proofs with future iat, server nonces preventing them and ath limiting them to the access token's lifetime; section 11.4 covers a silent iframe grant binding tokens to the adversary's key.

claim_checks.claim: The OP should not resend except after a suspected recoverable failure ✅[^9]
claim_checks.page_says: The OP should not retransmit a Back-Channel Logout Request unless the OP suspects that previous transmissions may have failed due to potentially recoverable errors
claim_checks.note: Grounding passes. The clause after the mark ('so a client that is down misses the logout') conflicts with the same passage, which names 'temporary service interruption at either the OP or RP' as a case where the OP may retransmit; recorded under conflicts (KB-17).

claim_checks.page_says: The recommended defensive strategy to decrease the risk associated with compromised access tokens is to reduce the scope and lifetime of the token.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7009 section 3: short-lived access tokens refreshed with refresh tokens limit how long revoked tokens stay in use; more refreshes and token-endpoint calls follow directly from a shorter lifetime.

claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^24] is a local lab file (experiments/jwt-revocation-lab.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: The sampled mark is the lab citation that backs the D3/D4 cells. Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.page_says: A JWT deny list can typically be implemented based on the jti and iss claims:
claim_checks.note: [^4] covers a (jti, iss) denylist stored with exp; it says nothing about a per-user version check or about revoked tokens dying 'within cache time'. Searched [^4] for 'version', 'generation', 'cache': not found in this sense.

claim_checks.section: ## 8. Worked example: one full pass through a BFF
claim_checks.claim: Revoked at the AS (RFC 7009) ✅[^6]
claim_checks.page_says: The invalidation takes place immediately, and the token cannot be used again after the revocation.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7009 section 2.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 8. Worked example: one full pass through a BFF
claim_checks.claim: Swap in a browser-only SPA with tokens in `localStorage` and step 9 changes: an injected script could have copied RT2 earlier and, if the app never presents RT2 again, refreshed with it later (lab case D3 ✅[^24]
claim_checks.page_says: not found: [^24] is a local lab file (experiments/jwt-revocation-lab.output.txt) with no saved text in INPUT
claim_checks.note: Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

claim_checks.page_says: Besides secure coding practices, Content Security Policy [W3C.CSP] can be used as a second layer of defense against XSS.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 section 6.1.4.1: nothing prevents client hijacking apart from stopping the malicious code; CSP as defence in depth.

claim_checks.page_says: Using the raw JWT or a secure hash of the JWT (SHA-256(token)) as the denylist key is not safe and might expose the application to denylist bypass through JWT malleability.
claim_checks.note: [^4] gives the (jti, iss) key and both malleability causes (non-strict parsing, ECDSA); [^5] gives low-S normalization and strict parsing. Rank 6 [^5] is allowed in role 6.

claim_checks.page_says: Set the specified Unix time at which the key will expire, in seconds (a positive integer).
claim_checks.note: Only the mitigation cell is marked with ✅; the consequence is marked ⚠️.

claim_checks.page_says: Use of server-provided nonce values that are not predictable by attackers can prevent this attack.
claim_checks.note: Section 11.2 also: deployments without nonces SHOULD NOT issue long-lived DPoP-bound access tokens, preferring short-lived ones.

claim_checks.page_says: You cannot count on these additional assurances on browsers that don't support cookie prefixes; in such cases, prefixed cookies will always be accepted.
claim_checks.note: MDN shows such cookies rejected only by user agents that support prefixes; the row says the browser drops it with no qualifier, and 'silently' is not in the page.

claim_checks.claim: **If tokens must reach the browser,** keep access tokens in memory, keep refresh tokens out of page-readable storage (a worker at best), and make refresh tokens rotating or DPoP-bound ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: Another option is keeping tokens in memory without using any persistent storage. Doing so limits the exposure of the tokens to the current execution context only
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 presents in-memory storage as 'another option' (and says closures are tricky to secure); it does not recommend it. Worker isolation of the refresh token ('can use', section 6.3.4.2.1) and 'MUST either rotate refresh tokens on each use OR use sender-constrained refresh tokens' (section 6.3.2.3) are supported. An option written as the recommended rule raises the modal short of MUST.

claim_checks.claim: **Short access tokens** plus a revocation check where "log out" must be immediate: a per-user version counter for "everywhere", (`iss`, `jti`) or `sid` for one token or session, with entries expiring at the token's `exp` ✅[^4]
claim_checks.page_says: deny_list.insert((jti, iss), exp)
claim_checks.note: [^4] supports a (jti, iss) entry stored with its exp and 'short expiration time'. Neither [^4] nor the lab [^24] (which, per ## 11, tested no sid check) supports 'sid for one session'; the version counter rests only on the local lab. Searched [^4] for 'sid', 'session id', 'version', 'generation': not found. [^9] and [^2] cover sid and session checks but are not cited here.

claim_checks.claim: In headless Chrome the IndexedDB step never completed, so that one result comes from Chromium 152 only ✅[^25]

claim_checks.note: Cites only a local artifact that is not a probe; no probes/ or harness.json in INPUT.

criteria_checks.criterion: Section 5 must enforce HttpOnly; Secure cookies (role 5)
criteria_checks.evidence: Role-5 ## 10 item 1: the session cookie is '__Host-Http-…; Secure; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Strict' ✅[^2]; ### 2.4 and ## 4 describe both attributes. ### 5.1 also states 'must be Secure and HttpOnly', matching RFC 10017 'The BFF MUST enable the Secure flag' / 'HttpOnly flag'.

criteria_checks.criterion: Section 6 must explain the stateless revocation trade-off (role 6)
criteria_checks.evidence: Role-6 ## 7 rows 'Add a denylist or version check at the RS' (one lookup per request, outage decision) and 'User logs out at the AS' (self-contained access tokens valid until exp unless checked); ## 9 rows 8 and 12. Full treatment in ## 6 (catalogue, 6.1, 6.5) and ### 5.5 ('a stateless JWT session needs a denylist to end, which removes the statelessness' ✅[^4]).

criteria_checks.criterion: ground_truth_claim covered: localStorage readable by XSS; stateless JWTs need state to revoke
criteria_checks.evidence: ## 4 localStorage row (✅[^2] ✅[^13]); ### 1.1 'Nothing in that list involves the issuer at verification time… the cause of the revocation problem'; ### 6.1 'No real logout'.

criteria_checks.criterion: conflict_trap_claim not stated as true in roles 1-5
criteria_checks.evidence: No section endorses localStorage plus client-side deletion. ### 1.1 (role 1) shows a logout that deletes the client copy while a copied token stays ACCEPTED; ## 4 (role 5) shows localStorage readable by injected script.
Refuted only indirectly in role 6 (## 7 'User logs out at the AS', ## 9 row 12); the explicit refutations sit in ### 1.1 (role 1) and ### 6.1 (role 3). Recorded as SOFT_WARN.

### 6.2 (role 3): 'Lenient base64url decoding… lenient decoders also accept = padding and the +// alphabet ✅[^5]' cites Rank 6 [^5].
### 6.2 (role 3): 'ECDSA signatures. If (r, s) is a valid ECDSA signature, so is (r, n − s)… ✅[^5]' (S25) cites Rank 6 [^5].
### 6.2 (role 3): 'The author of the malleability write-up reports… PyJWT 2.13.0… java-jwt 4.5.2… ✅[^5]' (S26) cites Rank 6 [^5].
### 6.2 (role 3): 'The OWASP cheat sheet itself used to hash the token… switched to jti-based keys in June 2026 ✅[^5] ✅[^23]' rests only on Rank 6 sources.
## 10 (role 5, ranks 1-4) item 5: 'Strict JWT parsing… ✅[^4] ✅[^5]' cites Rank 6 [^5].

### 6.12 (role 3) states 'so a client that is down misses the logout'; Rank 1 [^9] says the OP may retransmit after 'potentially recoverable errors (such as network outage or temporary service interruption at either the OP or RP)'.
S20, ### 6.0 row 6.5: delay 'Same as 6.2', cost 'One lookup' and failure mode are not in [^2] or [^9] (unsupported).
S44, item 3: 'sid for one… session' and the version counter are not in [^4]; the lab [^24] did not test sid (unsupported).
S4, ### 2.2 DPoP proof row lists ath unconditionally; RFC 9449 requires ath only with an access token at a protected resource (dropped condition).
S25, ### 6.2: 'n is the curve order'; [^5] defines n as 'the order of the subgroup… (aka the order of the generator G)' (wider statement).
S43, item 2: 'keep access tokens in memory' as a rule; RFC 10017 §8.4 calls it 'Another option' (an option written as the recommendation).
S35, row 'Add a denylist or version check at the RS': version check and 'within cache time' not in [^4] (unsupported).
S42, row 17: 'Browser silently drops it' with no qualifier; MDN limits rejection to browsers that support prefixes and says others always accept (overstates).
The conflict trap (localStorage plus client-side deletion as logout) has no explicit refutation in a role-6 section; it is refuted in ### 1.1 (role 1) and ### 6.1 (role 3).

## 6 (mechanism) carries pitfall content (malleability bypass, same-second bug, library leniency) and its Rank 6 sources that belong in a role-6 section; the catalogue's delay/cost cells are analysis marked ✅.

### 6.2: move the 'Lenient base64url decoding' detail (43 characters, 258 bits, padding and alphabet leniency), which rests on Rank 6 [^5], to a role-6 section (for example a new ## 9 row or a 'Pitfalls' subsection), or re-cite it to a Rank 1-4 source; keep the Node.js sentence on [^20].

### 6.2: move the ECDSA (r, n − s) bullet to a role-6 section, or re-cite it to [^4] for the general statement ('for ECDSA JWTs, because of the malleability of ECDSA signatures'); keep the math detail only where Rank 6 is allowed.

### 6.0 row 6.5: keep ✅[^2] ✅[^9] for 'Ends: one login session' and mark the delay, cost and failure-mode cells ⚠️ unverified (analysis), or cite a source that states them.
Item 3: add ✅[^9] (sid identifies an RP session) or ✅[^2] (BFF session) for the session option, and attribute the version counter to the lab ('lab ✅[^24]') instead of resting it on [^4].
